sources.entry: 2. Optimizing software in C++ - Maps C++ onto pipeline mechanisms and shows why a loop-carried dependency chain, not instruction count, paces a loop.

summary.title: Optimizing software in C++ (Agner Fog)
summary.one_liner: Learn how C++ constructs, compilers and x86 CPU pipelines affect speed, and why loop-carried dependency chains often limit loop performance more than instruction count.
takeaways: Software is often slow because of wasteful tools, frameworks and abstraction layers, not CPU limits; reducing abstraction makes performance easier to reason about.
Use a profiler to find hot spots and focus optimization effort on the most time-consuming parts of a program.
Section 3.15 and 3.16 cover dependency chains and execution unit throughput as limits on speed.
The manual covers costs of C++ constructs (integers, floats, branches, loops, virtual functions, templates, threads) and how compilers optimize them.
It targets advanced programmers on x86 Windows, Linux and Mac; the first of five Agner Fog optimization manuals.
summary.summary: This is the first of five optimization manuals by Agner Fog, aimed at advanced C++ programmers on x86 platforms (Intel, AMD, VIA) under Windows, Linux, BSD and Mac OS X. The table of contents covers choosing platforms and compilers, finding time consumers with profilers, the cost of C++ constructs, compiler and CPU optimization obstacles, memory and cache access, multithreading, out-of-order execution, SIMD vector operations, CPU dispatching, and testing speed. The text in this excerpt is the introduction and early sections; the listing's claim about loop-carried dependency chains corresponds to section 3.15 and the out-of-order/pipeline material, which were not in the provided text. The approach is based on study of compiler and microprocessor behaviour, with concrete guidance on code constructs.
